Let $h,a,\rho_0,\mu>0$, $p_0,G,V_0,V_1\in\mathbb R$, and $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. Use SI units: lengths in metres, $p_0$ in pascals, velocities in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, density in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, viscosity in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, pressure in pascals, and $G$ in pascals per metre. Let $e_x,e_y,e_z$ be the standard Cartesian unit vectors. In Cartesian coordinates, $\operatorname{div}u=\partial_xu_x+\partial_yu_y+\partial_zu_z$ and $(\Delta u)_i=\partial_{xx}u_i+\partial_{yy}u_i+\partial_{zz}u_i$. The stress is $\sigma=-pI+2\mu D$, with $D=(\nabla u+\nabla u^{\mathsf T})/2$ and $(\nabla u)_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$. The selected constant-density incompressible Newtonian model has
$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

For the infinite plane channel
$\Omega_{\rm ch}=\{(x,y,z):x,z\in\mathbb R,\ 0<y<h\}$, set
$u=(v(y),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, with $v\in C^2([0,h])$ and wall values $v(0)=V_0$, $v(h)=V_1$. The unique profile within this one-dimensional ansatz is
$$v(y)=V_0+(V_1-V_0)\frac yh+\frac{G}{2\mu}y(h-y).$$
Its volume flux per unit width in $z$, measured in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and channel shear values are
$$Q_{\rm ch}=\int_0^h v(y)\,dy=\frac h2(V_0+V_1)+\frac{Gh^3}{12\mu},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(0)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}+\frac{Gh}{2},\quad \sigma_{xy}(h)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}-\frac{Gh}{2}.$$

For the infinite circular pipe
$\Omega_a=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ y^2+z^2<a^2\}$, take $x$ as axial coordinate, $r=(y^2+z^2)^{1/2}$, $u=(w(r),0,0)$, and $p=p_0-Gx$. Require $w(a)=0$ and require the radial field $(y,z)\mapsto w((y^2+z^2)^{1/2})$ to be $C^2$ on the closed disk. The unique profile within this ansatz is
$$w(r)=\frac{G}{4\mu}(a^2-r^2),\qquad Q_{\rm pipe}=\int_0^a2\pi r\,w(r)\,dr=\frac{\pi Ga^4}{8\mu}.$$
The pipe volume flux is in $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$. For $r>0$ let $e_r=(0,y/r,z/r)$ and define the radial-axial stress component by $\sigma_{rx}=e_r\cdot\sigma e_x$; it is $\sigma_{rx}(r)=\mu w'(r)=-Gr/2$.

Both fields satisfy the exact stationary Navier–Stokes equations for every allowed parameter choice and also the corresponding steady Stokes equations because their time derivatives and convective accelerations vanish. Uniqueness is only within the stated ansätze; pipe uniqueness uses full-disk regularity at the axis. These infinite or fully developed geometries give no finite entrance or exit error estimate, stability or transition claim, observation, or empirical-validity claim.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Let $d\ge2$ be an integer, and let $L>0$ be the numerical period in a fixed

real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$. For $s\ge0$, let
$$H^s(\mathbb T_L^d)=\left\{f\in L^2:\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^s|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with norm given by the square root of this sum; the weight is dimensionless.
Under Countable Choice the coefficient map is injective, so this is a norm.
The real solenoidal spaces are
$$H=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d): k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\text{ for every }k\ne0\},\qquad V=H\cap H^1(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d).$$

Fourier-basis theorem makes the coefficient map a surjective isometry from

equivalence between Fourier divergence and distributional divergence in this
definition use that hypothesis. Under the same assumption, the orthogonal

$P_0=I$ and

$N\ge0$, rectangular truncation $\Pi_N$ keeps precisely $|k|_\infty\le N$. A weak
derivative in coordinate $j$ has Fourier coefficient $i\kappa_{k,j}\widehat f(k)$.
For $r>0$, $H^{-r}$ is the Hilbert completion of finite complex Fourier

$\sum_k(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^{-r}|\widehat f(k)|^2$; its real subspace is the

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

Their absolute-value seminorms therefore belong to the test topology defined in the Statement, so $u,T$ are spacetime distributions and their derivatives use the stated transpose convention. The quadratic map $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ is continuous from $L^2_x$ to $L^1_x$, making each Fourier coefficient measurable and bounded on finite time intervals. The multiplier formula defines $\widehat\pi(k,t)$; its coefficients are bounded in $k$ by $C_d\|u(t)\|_2^2$. Repeated spatial integration by parts gives rapid uniform decay of smooth-test Fourier coefficients. The pairing series for $\pi$ is absolutely convergent and bounded by a finite-order test seminorm, hence continuous in the stated test topology and zero at the spatial mean mode.

u\Delta u=0$ after testing against solenoidal fields. Adding the displayed gradient identity yields $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}T+
abla\pi-
u\Delta u=0$ for every smooth periodic vector test, which is the claimed equation.

If $\pi_1,\pi_2$ are two such mean-zero distributions, their difference $Q$ has zero spatial gradient. Its $k$th spatial Fourier coefficient, a distribution in time, therefore vanishes for every $k\ne0$ since $i\kappa_k\ne0$; its zero coefficient vanishes by the mean-zero normalization. Thus its rectangular Fourier partial sums converge to $\phi$ in the smooth test-function topology. $$p_{K,m}(\phi)=\max_{j+|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{(t,x)\in K\times\mathbb T_L^d}|\partial_t^j\partial_x^\alpha\phi(t,x)|\qquad(m\in\mathbb N_0);$$
equip $\mathcal D_{\rm per}(U)$ with the locally convex inductive-limit
topology over these fixed-time-support spaces, generated by all seminorms whose
restriction to every fixed-time-support space is continuous. A spacetime distribution means a
continuous complex-linear functional on this test space; all pairings are
bilinear, and derivatives act by transposing the corresponding test derivative
with a minus sign. Then there is a unique mean-zero-in-space
distribution $\pi$ on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb T_L^d$ such that
$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)+\nabla\pi=\nu\Delta u$

coefficient to vanish. Specifically, for $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, its $k$th spatial
Fourier coefficient is the time distribution defined by
$\langle\widehat\pi(k),\psi\rangle=\langle\pi,\psi(t)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\rangle$
for $\psi\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb C)$, with the spacetime
distribution pairing taken using $dt\,L^{-d}dx$ and extended complex-linearly;

Let $d\ge2$ be an integer, and let $L>0$ be the numerical period in a fixed
length unit. Let
$\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure
$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ put
$\kappa_k=2\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\exp(i\kappa_k\cdot x)$. For a complex
scalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let
$\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx$;
real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$. For $s\ge0$, let
$$H^s(\mathbb T_L^d)=\left\{f\in L^2:\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^s|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with norm given by the square root of this sum; the weight is dimensionless.
Under Countable Choice the coefficient map is injective, so this is a norm.
The real solenoidal spaces are
$$H=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d): k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\text{ for every }k\ne0\},\qquad V=H\cap H^1(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d).$$
The zero Fourier mode is unrestricted. Under Countable Choice, the supplied
Fourier-basis theorem makes the coefficient map a surjective isometry from
$L^2$ onto $\ell^2$; the coefficient-space norm identifications and the
equivalence between Fourier divergence and distributional divergence in this
definition use that hypothesis. Under the same assumption, the orthogonal
solenoidal projection $P$ is well-defined on $L^2$ and has multiplier
$P_0=I$ and
$P_k=I-\kappa_k\kappa_k^{\mathsf T}/|\kappa_k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. For integer
$N\ge0$, rectangular truncation $\Pi_N$ keeps precisely $|k|_\infty\le N$. A weak
derivative in coordinate $j$ has Fourier coefficient $i\kappa_{k,j}\widehat f(k)$.
For $r>0$, $H^{-r}$ is the Hilbert completion of finite complex Fourier
coefficient sequences in the norm squared
$\sum_k(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^{-r}|\widehat f(k)|^2$; its real subspace is the
completion of the conjugate-symmetric sequences.

Let $I$ and $J$ be intervals, possibly open at finite or infinite singular ends, and let $\phi:I\to J$ be a monotone differentiable surjection. Assume $\phi'$ is locally Riemann integrable and the proper change-of-variable hypotheses hold on every compact truncation. If $f$ is locally Riemann integrable on $J$, then
$$\int_J f(x)\,dx\quad\text{and}\quad\int_I f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt$$
converge simultaneously and, when convergent, are equal. At several singular ends this assertion is applied separately to the corresponding ends; orientation is retained for decreasing parametrizations.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
(A continuous function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable, by Heine-Cantor and Riemann's criterion).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:[a,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval
$[a,R]$ with $R>a$. If the improper Riemann integral
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx$$
converges in the sense of [[def-improper-integral-at-infinity]], then $f$ is
Lebesgue integrable on $[a,\infty)$ and
$$\int_{[a,\infty)} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n>0$, $u\in\mathbb R^3$, $T>0$, particle mass $m>0$, and Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$. Set $\theta=k_BT/m$ and define $M_{n,u,T}(v):=n(2\pi\theta)^{-3/2}\exp(-|v-u|^2/(2\theta))$. Its Lebesgue moments are
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}M_{n,u,T}\,dv=n,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^3}vM_{n,u,T}\,dv=nu,$$
$$m\int_{\mathbb R^3}(v-u)\otimes(v-u)M_{n,u,T}\,dv=nk_BT\,I_3,\qquad \frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v-u|^2(v-u)M_{n,u,T}\,dv=0,$$
and
$$\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v|^2M_{n,u,T}\,dv =\frac{mn|u|^2}{2}+\frac{3nk_BT}{2}.$$
Thus its pressure tensor is isotropic and its centered heat flux vanishes; these conclusions concern this Gaussian profile and do not impose isotropy on a general kinetic density.

Adopt Countable Choice, denoted $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval measured in seconds, let $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ be periods measured in metres, and let
$$\Omega:=\prod_{j=1}^3(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z).$$
Write $C:=\prod_{j=1}^3[0,L_j)$ and let $\pi:\mathbb R^3\to\Omega$ be the quotient map. Define $dx$ on Borel subsets $E\subseteq\Omega$ by
$$dx(E):=\lambda_3(C\cap\pi^{-1}(E)),$$
and use its completion as the spatial measure. Thus $dx$ is the pushforward of three-dimensional Lebesgue measure restricted to the half-open fundamental cell $C$, is not divided by the cell volume, and satisfies $dx(\Omega)=L_1L_2L_3$. Velocity $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is measured in metres per second and $dv$ is three-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Time integration uses Lebesgue measure $dt$ on $I$; product integrals use the corresponding product measures. In this definition $f\,dx\,dv$ is a number count, so a density $f$ has units $\mathrm m^{-3}(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^{-3}$.

Set $v_*:=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For $k=2,3$, define the dimensionless polynomial weight $\omega_k(v):=\sum_{j=0}^k(|v|/v_*)^j$. A kinetic density is a finite-valued measurable function $f:I\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ for which, at every $(t,x)$ under discussion,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3(v)f(t,x,v)\,dv<\infty.$$
Define number density $n:=\int f\,dv$ and mass density $\rho:=mn$ for a fixed particle mass $m>0$ in kilograms. Where $n>0$, define
$$u:=\frac1n\int_{\mathbb R^3}vf\,dv,\qquad c:=v-u,\qquad T:=\frac{m}{3k_Bn}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|c|^2f\,dv,$$
for a fixed Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in joules per kelvin. The velocity is $u$ in metres per second and the temperature is $T$ in kelvins. Where also $T>0$, define the candidate monatomic Maxwellian
$$M_{n,u,T}(v):=n\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_BT}\right)^{3/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{m|v-u|^2}{2k_BT}\right).$$
Its normalization and moments are established by a separate proposition; this formula is a definition here. At $n=0$, $u$ and $T$ are undefined, and statements using them assume $n>0$. A zero centered second moment gives $T=0$ and does not define the positive-temperature Maxwellian.

Define the pressure tensor, heat-flux vector, and kinetic-energy density by
$$P:=m\int_{\mathbb R^3}c\otimes c\,f\,dv,\qquad q:=\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|c|^2c\,f\,dv,\qquad E:=\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v|^2f\,dv.$$
Here $(a\otimes b)_{ij}=a_i b_j$. The finite absolute third moment makes these integrals finite. Their SI units are respectively pascals, watts per square metre, and joules per cubic metre. This is the monatomic translational model: no internal rotational or vibrational degrees of freedom and no isotropy assumption are included.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

Let $v_*=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\omega_3(v):=\sum_{j=0}^3(|v|/v_*)^j$, let $\tau>0$ be a relaxation time in seconds, and let $\epsilon>0$ be dimensionless. Let $f_0:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable velocity density with units fixed by the kinetic-density definition, with $\int\omega_3f_0\,dv<\infty$, number density $n>0$, and strictly positive centered second moment. Let $M=M[f_0]$ be its positive-temperature Gaussian from the single-species BGK definition. Fix a constant reference density $f_{\rm ref}>0$ with the same units as $f_0$ and assume $\int f_0|\log(f_0/f_{\rm ref})|\,dv<\infty$, with $0\log0:=0$ and the integrand $f_0|\log(f_0/f_{\rm ref})|$ assigned value zero where $f_0=0$. Define
$$f^\epsilon(t,v):=M(v)+e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}(f_0(v)-M(v)),\qquad t\ge0\text{ in seconds}.$$
Then $f^\epsilon\ge0$, has the same mass, momentum, and kinetic energy as $f_0$ for every $t$, belongs to $C^1([0,\infty);L^1(\omega_3\,dv))$, and solves, as an equality in $L^1(\omega_3\,dv)$,
$$\partial_t f^\epsilon=\frac{M[f^\epsilon]-f^\epsilon}{\epsilon\tau},\qquad f^\epsilon(0)=f_0.$$
A solution means a nonnegative $C^1([0,\infty);L^1(\omega_3\,dv))$ function satisfying this equality at each time. The solution is unique among nonnegative solutions in this function class whose density and temperature remain strictly positive. Moreover,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f^\epsilon(t)-M|\,dv =e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f_0-M|\,dv,$$
and for every $T_*>0$,
$$\int_0^{T_*}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f^\epsilon-M|\,dv\,dt \le\epsilon\tau\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f_0-M|\,dv.$$
Thus the equilibrium limit is exact for each fixed $t>0$ and in spacetime weighted $L^1$, but need not be uniform at $t=0$. This branch has stationary homogeneous Euler moments; it gives no evolving inhomogeneous Euler limit.

Each factor $g_{\mu_i,\sigma_i}(v_i)=(2\pi\sigma_i^2)^{-1/2}e^{-(v_i-\mu_i)^2/(2\sigma_i^2)}$ has mass one, mean $\mu_i$, and centered second moment $\sigma_i^2$ by [F1]–[F2]. Product Fubini [F3] therefore gives mass $n$, mean $\pm ae_1$, and covariance $\Sigma$ for each $G_{\pm ae_1,\Sigma}$. Their equal mixture has mean zero and covariance
$$\Sigma+a^2e_1\otimes e_1=\operatorname{diag}(\theta,\theta,\theta)=\theta I_3.$$
Its moments identify the target as $M_{n,0,T}$ with $k_BT=m\theta$ by [F4]. Since $\Sigma$ is positive definite, eigenvalue bounds give constants $C,c>0$ such that $f_0(v)\le C e^{-c|v|^2}$ and $f_0(v)\ge C^{-1}e^{-C(1+|v|^2)}$. Hence $|\log(f_0/f_{\rm ref})|\le C'(1+|v|^2)$ and the absolute entropy and weighted third moment are finite by [F6] and [F3].

Along $v=(s,0,0)$, the mixture is a positive constant times
$$e^{-s^2/(2(\theta-a^2))}\cosh\!\left(\frac{as}{\theta-a^2}\right).$$
The second derivative of its logarithm contains
$$\left(\frac{a}{\theta-a^2}\right)^2 \operatorname{sech}^2\!\left(\frac{as}{\theta-a^2}\right),$$
which is nonconstant because $a>0$. The logarithm of any Maxwellian is quadratic with constant Hessian, so $f_0\ne M$. By [F7], the weighted distance at time $t$ is $e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}C$ with $C:=\int\omega_3|f_0-M|\,dv>0$. It tends to zero for each fixed $t>0$, equals $C$ at $t=0$, and its time integral is at most $\epsilon\tau C$. Therefore convergence is not uniform on $[0,T_*]$, while the stated spacetime convergence holds.
